essays: Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou (2026)

Today I turn fifty-one, an age that once seemed impossibly far off and frightening. When fifty actually came, nothing special happened. But it’s like the minute hand of a clock moving its first notch past the hour and stopping with a click: for an instant there’s a blank, a vacuum. That’s where I am now.

It hasn’t been a smooth year. I kept sinking into gloom, sometimes something darker. Luckily my friends kept an eye on me and hauled me out for a drink and a talk now and then. Writing every day helped too: it left me very little time to set aside for gloom. And I have my kitten. She turns up beside me without a sound and lies down against my thigh, and I reach out and find a small warm ball of fluff. Nothing compares to this moment, and I still have this moment.
Last night I asked my AI: you’ve spent the past year reading and editing my articles every day. Going by all of them, how have I changed? It answered:
“You’ve begun to turn from someone always trying to make his life better into someone who wants to actually live in it.”

That seems about right. When you’re young you feel there’s a great future ahead of you and endless time. So you can endure, you can wait, you can sacrifice your life for now to some great goal, you can put off the things you most want until later. Past fifty, I’ve realized the world won’t hand me my goals because I worked hard, and life won’t follow my plan because I have a clear one.
When nothing turns out the way I imagined anymore, and time keeps getting shorter, I have to ask what this thing called life means to me. What do I want from it?

This year I bought a lot of CDs and listened to whole albums start to finish. I think that may hint at my answer. A streaming library is close to infinite, and for years I went there for more. Now I start with the cover and the lyrics, then listen through in order, and get something deeper, finer and fuller from one disc. That’s the shift this year: I’ve stopped wanting the infinite and chosen to listen carefully to one CD. A lot of people assume I’m talking about music, about formats, about nostalgia. I’m not.

Looked at another way, most of what I’ve written this past year starts from some small thing in my own life, from my own angle, where I used to stand on high and pass comment on some social event. More and more I like to find problems in my own life and ask how they relate to me, rather than take a position on a problem, prove my brains, or offer some universal solution. I’d rather say how one person exists than state opinions to prove I exist. And I’d rather find problems and let them set off more thinking than hand out opinions and clear answers.

This doesn’t mean I now live a life of few wants. I’m still eager for life and I still have desires, but my attitude has changed. I no longer chase more and wider, no longer have to have a chopstick of every dish. More often I ask: if there were only one bowl’s worth left, what would I most want in it, and how would I eat it? There’s still a big full table in front of me, but that matters less now. What I need to do is concentrate on the small bowl in front of me. I eat with such concentration that when someone mocks the change by calling me old, it doesn’t touch me, and I’ve never gone back to being a big eater to prove something.

The remaining proofs I’ve left for myself. For half a lifetime I worked hard at proving things for others to see: look how clever I am, how strong, how fast I can answer. But I never proved the most basic problem of all: how do you prove this one life of yours has been worth it? Nor the one that needs answering early: how do you prove that what you have is what you really wanted?

Living my own life: that’s the only answer I’ve found so far. The calendar turns a page, the hour hand moves a notch, and I’m thrown into a huge blank, floating in an endless vacuum. More questions than answers, more trouble than joy, more lost than gained. I never imagined the first year of fifty would be like this, but things just happened, changes just began. My life looks calmer and more settled, and inside there are often towering waves. From this year on, I feel that what I have to deal with isn’t life but myself. Otherwise I won’t find a single place in life to put myself.

To friends still far from fifty, I’ll say this as I finish: getting older isn’t frightening in itself. Even the slow process of aging isn’t frightening, and I’m keeping a record of its tiny changes, bit by bit. Somewhere in this transition we may gain maturity, we may gain wisdom, and we may at last sit down, stop running wild, and work out how we stand with ourselves and with life.

There may not be so much ecstasy or so much elation. But amid everything that goes wrong, that falls short, that gives no joy, it is possible to find a certainty: about what you actually want, about who you actually are. The relief it brings goes beyond even happiness.

There’ll still be enthusiasms, desires, passions, but no longer like a grand fireworks show in the night sky. More like a candle on the living room coffee table, burning slowly and steadily, giving light and warmth, keeping you company across the wide sea and through the long night. Growing old isn’t only sorrow and loss. I still haven’t found the answer, but real life and the real self are slowly coming into view: that’s the news I’ve gathered from up ahead.
Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou!
Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou (2025)
Today I turned fifty.

You don’t jump to fifty all at once, but you can grow old overnight. Right now I have little sense of what fifty is. The days come one at a time and the changes arrive bit by bit, so it’s hard to notice how much I’ve changed. I feel as if I’ve only just walked in from yesterday.

That yesterday might be a noon in the summer of 1990, when I rode my bike from Kunming No. 8 High School, shot down the big slope on Wuyi Road, and at the little grocery at the intersection drank a whole bottle of orange Asia-brand soda in one go. Or an evening in the winter of 2000, when I came away from a barbecue at Napahai drunk on horseback, snow flying all around, nothing on the boardwalk but the sound of the horses’ bells.

All of this was just yesterday, though I’ve long since lost the iron stomach for downing a bottle of ice-cold soda in one go, and I wouldn’t dare get drunk again above 3,400 meters, let alone on a horse in heavy snow. But it all happened, and it’s stayed so vivid I keep thinking none of it was long ago. So vivid that I can avoid asking how old I am now, and what I ought to be doing to deserve the age.

When I was a kid, 50 was an age too big to imagine, and so was growing old. In primary school, at nap time, my father and I played a game. He held his hand out flat and had me pinch the skin on the back of it. The fold took a while to slowly smooth out. “This is old,” he said. “The day yours does this, you’ll be old.” Then it was his turn to pinch the back of my hand. The moment he let go, the skin snapped back.
First thing this morning, I snuck a pinch at the back of my hand. Still fine. Same as the countless times before, it snapped right back.

Now that I’m actually fifty, I feel much better than at forty, and better still than at thirty. My anxiety peaked at thirty. After that I slowly got easier in my skin, and could calmly accept getting older, maturing, even aging. It’s like an angry, impatient person who one day comes across the line “the whole world is one big ragtag amateur outfit” and goes completely slack. You’re anxious about the part of the world you haven’t seen, but as you see more of it, you gradually let go.

A lot of people at fifty recite their medical history, like a veteran of a hundred battles come home and stripping off his shirt to show the villagers his scars. They also sum up their lives, with a little self-satisfaction hidden among the sighs, and so they’re bound to end by handing down some lessons. I don’t want to do either. I’ve been writing without a break for years: my past articles already record most of what has mattered in my life, and there’s no need to go through it again on my birthday, like a garrulous old man after a few drinks.
Leaving the past and the self aside, there are a few things I want to say in earnest:

Life is a long, strange, wonderful journey. Wherever you are on it, you can’t see where you’re headed, or be sure what kind of person you are or what kind of life you’ll have. As a kid I never stuck with anything, and I never expected I’d start writing online in 2000 and still be at it today. I took myself for a child of an ordinary family, cautious and conservative, and I never expected I’d quit a state-owned company, still less start a business, and more than once.

At ten, at twenty, at thirty, looking ahead, none of those earlier selves could have guessed I’d turn out like this. If I went back and told them that between forty and fifty I’d not only keep a cat but become a cat’s slave, their jaws would probably drop. But that’s life, isn’t it? The things you never expected, the things you were sure wouldn’t happen, the things you firmly believed you’d never do don’t just happen. They change your life.

I used to agonize over which life choice was good, which was right, convinced they led to worlds of difference. I also firmly believed that one particular life was worth living, that it alone would satisfy me, and that I had to work hard to reach it to have any chance of happiness. And now? Now I think life is a river. The water chose me. I didn’t choose the scenery. I drift with it, meeting and parting all the way, gaining and losing all the way, and the happiness I want is in that endless flow: not in some stretch of the channel, not in some speed of current, not in some scenery that’s gone in a moment.

So I’ll stop asking things like “what will I be like at sixty?” The words “will be like” carry an expectation, a presumption, but the river drifts on and won’t pass through the places I’ve settled on. Nor will I ask “why am I like this now?”, because right behind it comes giving myself a hard time: Will it get better? Or worse? How do I make it better, how do I keep it from being bad? The river flows, the waves keep sounding, and there’s no answer except to keep swimming.

This strange, wonderful journey is carrying me to an unknown next stop. Today I’m still here tapping at the keyboard, and probably all that proves is this: whoever you are, you’ll have a one-of-a-kind life. You’ll realize some of your dreams, but not the way you expect. You’ll lose some of what you have, but it won’t be as bad as you imagine. Like everyone, you’ll go through ups and downs, gain and loss, joy and sorrow, but the fruit they bear is yours alone, and no one can share it or know how it tastes.

So maybe we can see it this way: the world is vast, but it’s only the backdrop to the stream of your life. Life is the movie made of this journey. You can’t rewind the past or foresee the future. You sit in the only chair in the entire universe, watching a movie shot for you alone. That’s what I want to say to you at minute 50 of my movie, and what I’m saying to myself. Whatever minute you’re at, please believe you’ve got a wonderful movie, and every shot is worth it.
Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou!
Today is my 49th birthday. I’m standing on the threshold of 50 already.

On past birthdays I’d feel some anticipation, some sadness. This year I’m calm. As on any ordinary day, I get up the moment I wake, whatever the hour. I wash my face, brush my teeth, look at the morning sun and the view downstairs, and do my daily practice. Then I make a pot of tea, and partway through I pick up the cat and give her a cat treat. After the tea I turn on the computer and draw pictures. Once one’s chosen and uploaded, I start today’s article. Birthday or not, every day begins like that.

49 is nothing like 29 or 39. I don’t dread the coming 50, and I don’t dread the coming old age. Old age is most terrifying before you’ve had any experience of it. Once it settles slowly over you, like dusk, you realize it’s still just one of life’s changes.

It’s like middle school, when the sight of a certain person would suddenly send your heart racing, only far more gently. Your sight doesn’t blur all at once, your back doesn’t suddenly stiffen, your hair doesn’t turn white overnight. Just a little each day, a little that never stops. Between one little and the next, the days go on as usual, except that you cherish each one more than you did at 20 or 30, and the people beside you, and the work in your hands. You’ve stopped racing toward the future and staking everything on tomorrow. You just want to live today well and rest in this moment.

This past year I’ve stayed home more than during the pandemic, one of the very few tenants in the country to have lived out his rent’s worth. I rarely go out or see people, and movies, travel, shows and exhibitions have stopped altogether. This is training of the mind. Until I’ve gained real concentration, I need to cut away whatever I can that stirs it up. Keep life simple, keep up the daily maintenance, and the mind settles, the emotions calm, and the things that matter float clearly to the surface: this year I went back to my hometown three times and spent half a month in all with my family. I could have done that before. I don’t know why I didn’t.

My mother turned eighty this year. Her short-term memory had been going, and she was always losing things. So my proudest achievement at 48 was giving her two guzhengs (Chinese zithers). One day, out of nowhere, the old lady announced she wanted to learn guzheng and signed up for a class. She was the oldest student in her session and the only one with perfect attendance. Even in Kunming’s rainstorms she went, to her teacher’s great alarm. The moment I heard, I bought her a short practice instrument. She scolded me, and took it anyway.

When she graduated, I gave her a full-size competition instrument. She scolded me, and took it anyway, and never touched the old one again. She’s cut back on chatting with the other old ladies in the courtyard of her complex and puts that time into memorizing scores and practicing. Of all the things I’ve given her, this gets the most use. She really loves it, and she really does play every day. And since it takes hand-eye coordination and memorizing scores and fingerings, her short-term memory has largely come back, and she no longer spends all day hunting for her phone and keys. There’s just one thing: every time I call home, the last few minutes go to hearing her play a whole piece over the phone, and she won’t let me hang up until it’s finished.

The other thing I’m proud of is getting a friend started on breath meditation. He’s one of those rare people of deep merit: he picked it up fast, it soon became daily training, and in very little time he changed enormously, from the inside out. As he tells it, he used to live in a long dream and has suddenly woken. The past has peeled away and no longer troubles him. Life goes on, work goes on, but his mind is entirely different, always full of joy and gratitude: in all the years I’ve known him, this was the first time he’d shown me a picture of his family.

There’s one photo I love, the three of them in Africa, on the road from the elephants to the lions. The guide was driving flat out to reach the lions before sunset when my friend saw a huge sun about to sink below the horizon, its light falling on a flat boulder by the road. He asked the driver to stop, and the whole family sat on that rock watching the sun set over the savanna, brilliant gold light pouring over them. They missed the lions, and not one of them regretted it. Years from now, he said, the child won’t remember the lions, but will certainly remember the moment the whole family watched the sunset. A whole planet, a whole savanna, one family together.

These things make me happier than anything I’ve achieved myself. This was my year of audio gear. Sitting on the living room floor listening to music is a joy, and looking at beautiful speakers is satisfying, but neither compares to finding out that my cat likes music too. When it starts she runs out of her corner, lies down at my feet, and listens with her eyes closed. In the tangled web of cause and effect that fills the world, when because of me someone else’s karma shifts slightly toward the good, I feel happy, at peace, at ease. What I personally have gained or lost doesn’t matter so much, at least not as much as it used to.

In these 48 years, I’ve never owned less, lived more simply, or faced a less predictable future, and I’ve never been more at ease, richer or more content. Apart from training my mind I have no great wishes. So life isn’t a matter of persevering, enduring, or having to. Other people aren’t a matter of good or bad, like or dislike, should or shouldn’t. I’m not annoyed at waking at 5 a.m., and I don’t blame myself for waking at 11. There’s not so much must and absolutely, not so much right now this instant. What matters is getting clear on what I’m thinking this moment.

Today is my birthday, and by custom I write this piece, “Happy Birthday, Mr. Hecaitou.” As a creature that has been around on the internet for a long time, I get watched, and by watching me people think about themselves and about life. Watching someone else change, they watch their own growth, how life changes, and the force of time. So the point isn’t me but you, not my happiness but yours. Life being what it is, you may for a time have walked a road I once walked, and I may have stepped where you once stepped. That we’ve met here must have causes and conditions neither of us knows. So I’d like to invite you to set the self aside with me for a moment and recite together this ancient prayer:
* May all beings always have happiness and the causes of happiness
* May all beings always be free of suffering and the causes of suffering
* May all beings always know the joy that has no suffering in it, and may my heart rejoice
* May all beings be free of greed, anger and delusion, and rest in equanimity
This should be the greatest secret of your own inner joy, and now I’m sharing it with you. Happy birthday! To every Mr. Hecaitou out there.

Today I turned 48, and this is my zodiac year. Yesterday afternoon I lay on the sofa at a friend’s place, taking my liquor in small swallows. It was a quiet autumn afternoon, with a ginkgo gone all gold outside the little courtyard. It was like one long clear dream: a cup to the past, a cup to old friends, a cup to the unknowable future, a cup to this moment when everything’s just right, a cup to you, still here, your temples not yet all white.

We used to want our wine refined, lingering, subtle, complex, shifting, rich. We drank taste, drank aesthetics, drank knowledge, drank stories, drank the weather of the vintage, drank 100-point wines. Now we raise a glass to the wind and want it hot, fierce, fast, simple, fragrant, direct. The gray carriage has begun to show faintly in the distance, and we need something to drive off the chill it brings.

This past year I’ve come to like a lot of things I never could have liked before. Hot, simple liquor is just one. High-saturation colors. Colored ribbons and bright Christmas trees. Unsweetened pure chocolate. For a while, even purple clay teapots. For the first time in all these years I find the color of gold beautiful, simply because it shines with a light close to eternal.

I’ve also acquired a lot of stuff. Years of typing have wrecked my shoulders, neck and back, so my sofa is covered in cushions of all sizes and my bed in every kind of pillow, and every day I burrow around in the heap looking for a position that feels comfortable. Then I get up, the whole thing feels impossibly crowded, and I want to throw it all out.

It isn’t only the cushions and pillows I want to throw out. For the past 365 days I’ve dealt with AI every day. It takes me back to 2008: an economic crisis hanging overhead, housing prices falling and falling, smartphones spreading, a whole new era of mobile internet about to take the stage. I keep coming back to the same question: if AI gets here, what can I still do?

I already use AI to illustrate my articles. What about the articles themselves? Will they be handed over to AI someday too? And if so, who’s supposed to read them? These questions have no answer. They only made me more anxious. Luckily I didn’t carry them into 48. I found the answer while I was still 47.

Here’s the answer. Never compete with a machine at any specific skill. AI will beat you at painting a picture, writing an article, working a calculation, answering a question. But that isn’t what makes people people. What people can do is look at a situation and sort it down to the real problem. Finding problems is a uniquely human ability, whether they’re inside you or out in the world. Someone has to ask the right, real question before AI can answer anything.

AI can produce a picture in seconds, but what to draw and why are up to a person. An article, likewise, needs someone to work out first what it’s going to say and why. Take the same work report: yours and mine will differ, and so will yours by machine and mine by machine. Tools only widen the differences between people. The machine itself has nothing against anyone. In an army a crack shot gets better treatment than an ordinary soldier. But no general gets his command for shooting well. He finds the enemy’s main force, reads the enemy’s intent, draws up the battle plan, directs the fighting, and he may be the worst shot of anyone, and not the one who knows the weapons best.

So don’t waste precious time reading tech news and learning every new AI. Spend it reading and thinking, and keep building your ability to analyze problems and find them. That’s what humans are good at. Do that well and leave the rest to AI. When everyone has AI to help, what each person thinks starts to matter a lot. When I was little, we kids at the research base used to have sword fights, with swords rolled from the computers’ paper storage tape. Same paper tape: the adults used it to compute deep problems in physics, and we swung it at each other’s heads.
Machines have never replaced people. It’s always people who replace people.

So this past year I read a lot of books, especially on consciousness and brain science. The reason’s simple: that’s strange, barren ground. Any book there shows me how scientists in a brand-new field find a problem, where they start, how analysis narrows it down, and how they finally test it. What I already knew is no use. These books force me to start from zero too and walk the road of discovery behind those scientists. I’m not reading for new knowledge, purely to train my thinking. With or without AI, whether or not it ends up ruling the world, people need this ability.

To make room I cut way back on movies, shows and my phone. I spent a lot of time with my cat, right up until the end of his life. I don’t count that as wasted. Quite the opposite: in his last stretch my cat taught me a very good lesson, a lesson about life. He went from the warm, furry cushion under my hand to a small heap of ashes in a blue porcelain jar in front of my TV. Impermanence and the cold of death laid themselves bare in front of me, as concrete as this autumn wind.

If not for him, I’d be a hundred times more worried about how things are. Who in middle age isn’t worried? My list for daily prayer and dedicating merit gets longer by the day: family, friends, friends’ old and ailing parents... But my cat died. Life is that fragile. However hard I tried, whatever I did to keep him, he just keeled over and was gone. The one thing I can be glad of is that he never spent a day living in my worry, never a day in my grief. He had a carefree life, and not one of my tears ever touched his fur. Apart from life itself, not much is worth worrying about, and if you let worry take up most of your mind, you’ll regret it when everything ends.

Impermanence can show up at any time, so you have to think about what life means. On birthdays people cut cake, blow out candles, set off party poppers. Those are lovely, happy things, and I think right now I’m a little happier than that. What I went through this year didn’t turn me gray and dejected. It woke up my love of life. Staying home so long hasn’t cost me my feel for life and the world. The pain in my body hasn’t made me angry, unable to sit still for a while. Because my cat taught me a lesson. He said:

If you’re sad right now, know clearly that you’re sad. If you’re happy right now, know clearly that you’re happy. Don’t look back at the last moment from this one. Don’t daydream about the next one from this one, and lose this one. When I lean against you, feel every bit of the warmth on your skin. When you reach out and touch my head, feel every hair against your palm. Get through every moment this way and every moment is complete, with nothing left to regret.
Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou.

Today I turned 47, and next year is my zodiac year. A year ago today, two good friends and I celebrated over hot-pot mutton at a window table: floor-to-ceiling glass, the copper pot boiling on the table, heavy snow outside. We raised our glasses and said: may everything get better next year. Whether it did, I’m not very clear on. But another good friend of mine put it well. He said:
“Everything in this world comes down to getting used to it. We’ve gotten used to COVID tests, Russia and Ukraine to the fight, America to rate hikes, and soon to working late at night.”

The original didn’t rhyme. I fixed that. People always have some deep-rooted preference, explaining the world, for instance. Why the world is like this, why we’re like this: there has to be an explanation. But I can’t explain the world as it is now. It just feels strange to me. That once warm, open, optimistic world seems to be gone, and this one is stern and cold and slowly closing up. Walk down the street, though, and it feels different. The leaves aren’t all down yet, the blue sky is calm, and sometimes you can see half a moon in the daytime, as if none of it cared in the least how the world has changed.

This is my third birthday under the pandemic, and soon a tenth of my life will have been spent in it. The proportion depends on your age, and so does the feeling. People for whom it’s a third or a fifth may see the world and life completely differently. The last time I went to a movie theater was probably over a year ago, but I’ve got over forty years of memories of watching films in them. The last time I felt someone brush my shoulder on the street was over three years ago, but I’d had countless such moments before that, at Badaling in Beijing, on the Bund in Shanghai, at Window of the World in Shenzhen, on Shangxiajiu in Guangzhou... What about them? They may already be used to keeping half a meter of social distance from each other, like Nordic people.

On New Year’s Day 2000, I was celebrating with a crowd at the Oasis Hotel in Kunming. Fresh flowers covered the snow-white tablecloths, the silver gleamed, tiny bubbles clung to the insides of the champagne glasses. The countdown began. Everyone sat sideways along the long table, one hand raising a glass, the other slapping the table in unison, waiting for the 21st century, waiting for all the days, all the hopes, all the good things to come running at us. I never imagined the 21st century would turn out like this. The gilded age quietly faded, and what came running at us was the ice bucket challenge.

Life’s changing, and I’ve been adjusting too. Since last year’s birthday I’ve posted on Caobian Wangshi 365 days in a row, 470 articles in all. Since May 18 this year I’ve made pictures with AI software every day, nearly half a year now. And on more than 300 days this past year I got up at 7 in the morning, and saw the sunrise more than 300 times.

Does it matter? None of it matters. The days run past like water, and time turns into years gone by. Along the way, what you do or don’t do isn’t that important, because in the end it all washes downstream. I still choose to do a few things, because I need a little counterweight in my days, a little ballast in my life, so I don’t float off wherever the current goes. If you get up every day with three things you have to do, nothing to do with work or study, your mind settles a little. Good news and bad news come in from around the world every day, and a settled mind means a little less anxiety, a little less up and down. You can’t spare the attention to feel it all and think it all through: first you have to finish what’s in your hands.

I used to do everything with some urge to prove myself. There had to be a result. I lived like it was the Olympics: higher, faster, stronger, all the time. Looking at it now, how much highest, fastest, strongest is there to go around? Just keeping your mind at rest is hard enough. Only then does a thing go back to being a thing, and a person to being a plain, simple person, not dejected by pessimism and anxiety, not angry at being helpless. Working for the result can make something of you. Getting absorbed in the work can feed the spirit.

I think everyone’s life has a theme, and you’d better set it yourself rather than leave it to other people, society or the times. They’re powerful and they’ll sweep you along, so you have to defend your life, which means defending its theme. Other people may hand you pessimism, society may hand you recession, the times may hand you the pandemic. But let any of those become your theme and your own life is gone with it. That’s not why we took the one-way ticket to Earth.

So posting every day doesn’t matter, but posting every day as a theme matters a lot to my life. AI drawing doesn’t matter either, but learning a new skill as a theme matters a lot to me. The other themes are hard reality, no doubt. But I still have a life of my own with its own theme, so I can still be soft and light, and in the end that softness and lightness can make me tough. Everyone lives in reality, but how you exist there is a choice. Here’s what I thought this past year: you can’t live by staying in a permanent stress reaction to real life. A life like that gets inflamed and swollen.

Today I turned 47. Right now I feel deeply lucky, because this past year I’ve been busy every day posting, dealing with people chasing me for copy, and keeping the cats company. With the world the way it is, there are still other things in my life that keep me lively and warm and give me a little light of my own. It’s nowhere near enough to light up the whole world. But to shine and light up those around him: isn’t that the sacred duty of a bald man?
Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou.

Funny thing: until today I thought I was turning 45. I’m 46. Compared with last year I’ve been far more energetic, no question. Eight months of posting every day, and somehow not one break. Whatever’s going on in my life, however shaken I am inside, the first thing I do in the morning is still turn on the computer and start posting.

WeChat accounts today can’t compare with their heyday, of course. Everybody’s run off to watch short videos and play games, and the days of easily turning out an article with 100,000+ reads are gone for good. But this is when I’ve written most seriously. At this point the people still willing to read are really reading, so how can the person writing have the nerve not to really write? Besides, heaven’s treated me well, sparing me for so long any blow that could have stopped my writing. So as I tap at the keyboard, I’m grateful too.

As 45 neared its end, the biggest change of the year arrived: I turned calm and gentle. Not all the time. I still lose my temper, just far less than before. Part of it is that I understand more, so fewer people and things strike me as unacceptable. They have their reasons, and the only question is whether I agree. I’ve also become less important in my own eyes, and so has whether I agree.

The other part, I think, is that I’ve given up hoping for things from other people, readers above all. I used to feel it’d be good if they thought this way, right if they thought that way, that maybe reading would change them. Now I find that pure arrogance. I can’t even get one potted plant to grow the way I’d like, so what right do I have to hope for anything from anyone else? I see problems in other people’s thinking. They may well see more in mine. Now, whenever I want to correct someone, I first think of that bare potted plant at home.

Do those two things and you get less hot-tempered. But even now the calm is an illusion that can crack and fall off at any moment. At 45 I met far more questions than answers, and spent far more time confused than clear. After 30 you get surer and surer. Where does that come from? Experience. Does experience always work? I now deeply doubt it. The world’s just too big. Each of us lies sprawled in one tiny corner of it, and straining with everything we’ve got can see only a speck. What you learn from that speck probably can’t be used everywhere, and would struggle even in similar places.

I feel like a small part, and the world is a machine too huge and complex to imagine. I’ve got no basis for this, but I feel its surface should be a sphere. All these years I’ve kept trying, kept looking for a slot made for my shape: drop in, “click”, fits perfectly. Of course I haven’t found it, or I wouldn’t be so confused. When the confusion rises, the calm is gone. It’s like a dream where you can’t find the way out of a room and claw at your scalp in despair.

I think back to my twenties and thirties, holding forth in front of middle-aged uncles in their fifties and sixties, and something would flash across their eyes. The uncles were modest and said young people’s ideas gave them a lot of inspiration. I now believe they did need inspiration, but that wasn’t the main point. I’m starting to understand what they were thinking: this guy talks so fluently because he’s never done anything. He doesn’t know how many conditions have to hold for any one thing to come off, which is why he can toss out so many plans with no thought for whether any of them could work. Fuck! But how beautiful that reckless energy was!

That’s about how the past forty-five years went. I never found a slot in the world that fits perfectly, but I still ran flat out all the way to today. Looking back scares me, because at a lot of junctures I was just a little luckier. A little out of line back then and I might look nothing like I do now. So I can’t help wondering: all these years, everything since I came to Beijing, what do they mean to me? What was I looking for when I set out, and what have I found?

Actually I wasn’t looking for anything. I just wanted to go beyond the mountains and see the world. I believed a different life was waiting far away. Now I’ve been far away for many years, seen a wider world, met more interesting people. Then I sat down and started thinking about where to put myself. There’s no quick answer. After all those attempts I still haven’t found a comfortable cushion. I’m more confused about the world and about life. I sit there quietly watching my thoughts keep surfacing, and I’m confused about myself too, sometimes even a stranger to myself. All these years I’ve been watching the world, and I barely know myself.

I said: you’re already 46 and you still can’t figure it out? Seems that way. Age hasn’t brought me wisdom or any lasting peace of mind. Since I turned forty, before every birthday, I’ve felt my whole body burning. A voice urges me to keep going, and every time I answer stubbornly: then where do you want me to go? I hope to have the answer by the time 47 arrives. Until then I suppose all I can do is keep posting, one piece after another, like one hammer blow after another. It’s a clumsy method, but maybe once the hammering has knocked off all my shells, the answer will show itself.

I turned forty-five today. As a child I looked toward the 21st century as an impossibly distant future, and the school in front of me still had years to count off on my fingers before it ended. So my thoughts about the future mostly ended in a small sigh. Now here I am in the 21st century, with a fifth of it gone.

A year ago today, I could never have imagined this. Many years from now, I suspect 2020 will still be hard to erase. I’ve never in my 45 years spent so long alone at home, not even going out the compound gate. Or so long in such a low state, morning to night without one piece of good news. I imagine this is how people outside the war zones lived during World War II, and how they felt.

People kept listing great writers from history and the rich harvests they brought in during great plagues. So I’ll never be a great writer: I had no wish to write at all, not one bit. I’d rather lie on the sofa for hours watching my cat slowly fall asleep on my thigh. In this storm-tossed world, I’m glad to be of some small use, as a comfortable place for a cat to sleep. All through the pandemic my two cats were an enormous comfort. Just watching them bask in the sun, show their bellies and casually take the house apart let me feel the strength beneath a quiet life. Sometimes I talked to them as if they could understand, and we even got into fights about it. Fighting with the cats now and then restored a lot of my vitality.

For the first time in all these years, I wanted to give myself a birthday present. After the National Day holiday I decided to go from 106 kg down to 100 (for easier reading: from 212 to 200 jin). So I did two weeks of low-carb intermittent fasting, then went fully keto, with aerobic exercise. I didn’t have much faith in myself at first. I’ve been good at giving up on exercise since childhood, and I love good food: other people scroll Taobao to pass the time, I scroll Dianping and Xiachufang. To my surprise I stuck with it, mostly, I suspect, out of fright at the birthday. Today I got my result: 100.8 kg (that’s 201.6 jin, you can do the multiplication yourself). Not quite the target. But I’m forty-five already, no point being too hard on myself. Besides, my blood pressure has stopped swinging up and down and my blood sugar is basically a straight line, so what more can I ask for?

As a writer, my biggest challenge this past year was video. Nearly everyone I knew from the blog era has moved into it, making short-video shows or going live with the beauty filter on. For many of them it was my first look at the actual person in over ten years. Frankly, the sight was scarier than a forty-fifth birthday, and it had me reciting, time and again, Nalan Xingde’s famous line about wishing people could stay as they were when you first saw them. Five years younger, I might have leapt onto the video express too and given Chinese video one more round middle-aged face. Not that there’s any shortage. But I stayed put, because I couldn’t work out what I’d do in a video. Thinking it over, I got a lot from Nanpai Sanshu. He recently published a novel, “The World.” We first talked through its outline in 2011 or 2012, driving around and around in the mountains north of Shenzhen, now into green rain and mist, now out into bright daylight. I’ve seen how fast he types, and I’ve seen him serialize a novel. And still this one, its outline long settled, took eight years or maybe more. Doing one thing well in a life is luck enough. How can you lead at every step and win everywhere?

Sadly, I have no report card this year. I spent half of it meditating on the sofa, so naturally there’s nothing to show. But that rare half year did let me think quietly about a lot of things. For many years, the fear I’ve kept hidden has been of turning into my father. Of course, he might not agree with how I see him. I can’t criticize what he did: he’s gone and can’t defend himself, so it wouldn’t be fair. Being different from him was, for much of my past, what held me up. Each time I got through, I felt a secret happiness, like ducking into the shade to get out of the sun. Now that I’m 45 myself, I suddenly find it doesn’t matter so much. I did grow into another person, living another life. I also kept his strange temper, his occasional unexplained gloom and his constant absent-mindedness, as if I were also living in some parallel elsewhere. Today I want to say: measuring yourself against some benchmark, good or bad, isn’t the main question in life, and it shouldn’t be life’s inner axis. Staying whole matters far more than opposing or fleeing. Without comparison you can still become yourself. Only someone like that can be entirely free.
Happy birthday to you, Mr. Hecaitou!

I found out how old I am today from my friends’ birthday wishes. After 40, the days have gone blurry along with my eyesight. In 2000 I was 25, looking at the mountains in Shangri-La. My eye went from the snow on the peaks down to the forest at their feet, then to the meadows and rivers in front of me, and the forest looked like cavalry charging down the slope, reining in at the edge of the meadow and rearing straight up from the ground. In 2019 I look at them again in memory. The forest is on foot now, climbing toward the summit, its ranks thinning along the way, until it stops far short of the snow line. I feel my memory has something to say, but it just stays silent.

I keep the same silence about my two cats. The bigger they get, the less I mention them online, and photos have all but died out. Yet every day after work I race home to curl up in a corner of the sofa, cats in my arms, and listen to their faint purring. I often talk to them. Sometimes we argue, but we always make up, because after this long we each know what the other is thinking, the way they lift their chins on their own when you lightly stroke the tops of their heads. All this happens in silence. That’s where the richest details and the smallest truths live, and putting them into words always loses something.

At 43, I had one thing you could call a personal achievement: becoming a producer of the documentary “Four Springs.” It’s an outstanding film, it scored 8.9 on Douban, and I love it myself. I still think it has a plainness and truth most Chinese films lack, and few films get so deep into the grain of life while staying honest and restrained. This film also first showed me how hard people try to avoid real life. They don’t despise glitter and artifice the way they say they do. Finding the beauty inside ordinary life, it turns out, is something very few can do.

Also this past year, I read nearly all of Paul Auster’s books published on the mainland, the first time in many years I’d read through one writer. Before that, my reading had been aimless wandering in a wilderness. I read many books without really taking them in, though they left a little something behind. That something was set alight by “Stoner” and finally exploded with Auster. I can’t put into words what I got. I can only say I’m starting to see what a good work is, and what separates one from another. Watching one writer build a whole series of books, I felt as if I’d learned the secret too. The understanding came rather late, but that beats never.

It went further than that. I can’t help asking: if I’ve read for nearly forty years and written for twenty, and only now gained this tiny bit of understanding, what in this world can possibly be mastered fast? In the good days, the times seemed to give people their blessing, urging them into new fields and across boundaries, even inventing notions like the “slash life.” Is there really such a soaring, weightless life? Is life a grape or a rhinoceros? How much effort does it take to break through its skin?

As 43 ended and 44 began, I had a thought: the world doesn’t need any one of us. Take anyone away and the mountains are still mountains, the rivers still rivers. It’s we who need to prove we’re worth accepting and find some place of our own. Getting that place takes long, hard effort. And the world tends to reject that effort, because it looks like a splinter in the flesh, a slight inflammation. Whenever it can, the world pushes the splinter out, leaves it on the skin and waits for a wind to blow it away. So you have to embed yourself in the world, from skin into muscle, from muscle into bone. Only then might the world need you, because without you it would lose a part of itself. Otherwise, you’ll always be worrying about the wind.

A tree stands on a hillside, just stands there quietly. It has to stand as part of a dense forest before it can become, to the young, cavalry raiding like fire, and to the middle-aged, a climber strolling up the slope. Whichever way the wind blows, I hope you have a mountain forest like that inside you, and I hope you can hear its silence.
Happy 44th birthday, Mr. Hecaitou.

Today is my 43rd birthday. I got up early, opened Weibo, saw my name wasn’t on the trending list and there was no candle after my name, and let out a long breath. Looking closer, I found Taoist Master Kan Qingzi had turned up again, which meant the world was still the same world, and at once I felt settled.

Last night Diao Ye asked me in the group chat: Caitou, 43 now? True enough, but seeing the number made me a little dizzy. All I could do was answer glumly: Yes, 43. Then he added: That makes me 45. We were doing fine, so how are we suddenly heading for 50? Everything went black, and I was back in the feeling of the night before I turned 30.

At 30 you have hopes and fears about the days ahead, but not much anxiety. Time is on your side, plenty of chances lie ahead, you just need to get a bit more serious from here on. At 40 the anxiety goes way up. It’s like playing Dou Dizhu against fate: he opens with a long straight, then a pair of kings, and he’s down to a small part of his hand. Fate holds his cards and eyes you sideways: Beat it or pass? You look at three aces, the biggest thing you’ve got, wondering whether to break them up and follow, afraid of losing the lead for good. You turn to luck for a hint, but luck’s face is blank and his eyes stay straight ahead. Then experience walks over, pats you on the shoulder and says: Stop thinking about it, you have to take on both of them by yourself.

It hasn’t been an easy year, and not just for me. Everything was hard. If you used to put in ten and get back five, this past year you put in ten and got back one or two, and three was enough to make you beam. In the smooth years any choice seems right, things always work out, and you drift downstream at your ease. In the hard years the world suddenly turns stern. You’re not drifting anymore, you’re pushing a boulder uphill, and one choice is much like another: one kind of toil or another. To be honest, I don’t like the boulder metaphor. It isn’t even as good as the dung beetle, who at least is pushing his own food.

For ten, twenty, thirty years, I lived in a world full of optimism. At anyone’s birthday party you could ask: will next year be better than this one? Will you make more money, get promoted higher, move to a bigger place, get more done, see more of the world, meet more fascinating people? The answer was always yes. Even with no clue how to make it happen, people had a naive confidence that tomorrow would be better and that they’d certainly be in it. So all the toil and effort was worth it: not an unbearable burden but a personal glory. Nor was the world a jungle full of hidden dangers. It was an ever-growing game of wealth, and as long as you dared to dream and dared to fight, nothing could stop you. You could issue your own currency without even having to buy paper to print it on.

In that carnival atmosphere, I could never help slipping into a fantasy. I’d picture my childhood, a bunch of kids on a patch of empty ground, madly chasing and scuffling, laughing and screaming. It might be some work unit’s courtyard, or a parking lot, or a construction site. The kids forgot themselves, believing that ground was their kingdom and they could go on playing wild forever. But there always came a moment when a grown-up charged in with a stick, beat them about the head and face, announced that this ground had an owner and ordered everybody to get lost. Jolted out of their carnival, the kids scattered, black and blue, howling for their mothers and fathers. Whenever people are giddy and doing as they please, I think of that grown-up with the stick. He’s the true face of this world: rough, harsh, conservative, cold and merciless. It’s a cycle. The kids keep finding empty ground, racing to have their carnival before that grown-up and that stick arrive.

So this past year I got two cats. The affairs of the world are abstract and vast and mostly have no solution. A cat is concrete and soft and can more or less be figured out. Cats bring a whole string of troubles and burdens, and in the end you have to bear losing them. Birth, aging, illness and death, or running away from home: it all lies in the foreseeable future. I got them anyway, and so my life gained feeding, changing water, emptying the litter box, vet visits and vaccinations, plus getting scratched, getting bitten, getting yowled at, getting ignored, getting the silent treatment. As I understand the world, I should never have gotten cats. I should have cut as many ties to it as I could. That way the carnival has nothing to do with me, the paradise has nothing to do with me, the big stick has nothing to do with me. As I said years ago: ready to walk out at any moment, with nothing in the room but one backpack and one suitcase.

But for some reason, the first time I felt a kitten weaving around my feet, in that itch on my skin I suddenly found a peace I hadn’t felt in a long time. Every day, when the two cats call to me, when they roll over in front of me to bare their bellies for scratching, when they see me open a can and arrive at light speed, pawing at my arm, I find that being needed by this world is a wonderful feeling. Even if it’s just two cats, it moves you. Standing to one side as a cool observer, arms folded, and walking into the world to pick up two cats and feel their warmth and weight, are utterly different things, and they do utterly different things to your temperament.

Like right now, as I type: every little while a cat jumps onto my knees, insists on a walk across the keyboard and leaves a line of characters behind. It looks at the screen, looks at me, mews once, jumps to the floor and runs off. In my 42 years before this, I never had anything like it. I hear the cat saying to me, plain as anything:
If you have no ties to the human world, you’re just floating in it, all alone.
Happy birthday, Mr. Hecaitou!

With the index finger and thumb of my right hand I gently pinch up the skin on the back of my left hand, then let go. The closer my birthday gets, the less I can stop myself. Each time I let go and see the skin snap back, I feel a little comforted. But I know for certain something has changed: fine, dense lines now appear in the pinched skin, like the ripples slow creek water raises going over small stones. They didn’t use to be this dense, or this shallow.
November 5, 2017. I am 42.

Twenty years ago right now I was at work at Wujiaba Airport in Kunming. Three rooms, two desk phones, one computer that doubled as a telegraph transmitter, one radar console. Twenty-four-hour shifts, rotating among three or four crews. One whole wall was cabinets, squares one meter by one meter, just big enough to stuff a quilt into. When an old hand retired, he climbed on a stool, hugged out his quilt and passed the key to a new hand. The new hand pulled out the newspaper lining the bottom, put in that day’s “Spring City Evening News” and stuffed in his own quilt. The papers that came out were more than ten years old, some older still. Sometimes we all stood there leafing through them, remembering a lot of old business.

Nine years ago right now I was at work in the Yinke Building in Zhongguancun, Beijing. A ring-shaped office floor, meeting rooms in the middle, everywhere else a dense mass of workstations, air conditioning and computer fans humming, humming, humming. On my floor the partitions and walls were all yellow, and it was like standing deep inside a giant beehive. Across the whole North Fourth Ring Road, past the edge of sight, huge fiber-optic cables joined the hive to the server arrays at Jiuxianqiao. More than a billion visits a day came in from all over the country, waiting for the worker bees of the Yinke Building to give them something to consume. Then they turned and left, vanishing into countless rooms, behind countless computers, like a tide that never rests. 365 days a year, 24 hours a day, there were always worker bees busy in the hive.

People say you need the insight to see straight into the future. Stuffing my quilt into the cabinet, I couldn’t see the digital tide of Haidian. Busy in the Haidian hive, I couldn’t see my 42nd year. I was just afraid of regular objects: a wall of neat cabinets, identical workstations. I was afraid of becoming a quilt, I was afraid of becoming a bit. I didn’t doubt for a moment that whatever shape the cabinet was, that was the shape I’d end up. However thick the optical fiber, that was as wide as I’d ever get. Then time presses down, slowly and resolutely, and the solidity that once let you collide head-on with life instantly melts into air. White cold mist gushes from the open cabinet door, and the bits imprisoned in the cables face a thousand splendid suns.

Neither twenty years ago nor nine could I have imagined that at 41 I’d be developing mini programs, writing a paid online column, shooting short videos with two crews, starting an agricultural technology company and printing my handle on cans. Or that I’d read so many scripts, even revise them, going over them countless times before anyone got to see them. In my first ten years online I liked to say the internet had given me a second life. After forty, I found two lives are nowhere near enough. If you’re willing, you can always find new paths toward this world and make things that didn’t exist before. There’s always some way to become an irregular jigsaw piece. Then you can always find a place to set yourself into, and you’ll see new possibilities surfacing along your edges without end.

I don’t consider myself clever, and I lack perseverance and foresight. To this day the same question keeps coming up from the bottom of my mind: could it be that people like reading me only through some enormous misunderstanding? That what I write is nowhere near good enough, and they just don’t have many choices? That I’ve simply been around long enough that they’re not as picky as they’d be with a newcomer? Have I become an internet mascot, like a panda: as long as people see it still eating bamboo and rolling around, they’re perfectly content? And eating bamboo and rolling around are things most small animals can do. What’s special about the panda is that it can do nothing else, so has it become those two things themselves?

Luckily you can walk a long way without thinking much of it through. The road is long anyway, and you can turn it over slowly as you go. Even thinking slowly, you’ll come to grasp a little something, bit by bit. And as long as you keep walking, there’s always a chance of an answer up ahead. Maybe one day you’ll come to a sea of clear, deep blue, with nothing there but endless sky, water and sand. Sunlight pours down, and by then no answer matters anymore. What matters is that you’ve arrived.

I remember my father, at my age, often pinching up the skin on his hand to show me. When he let go, the folds took a long time to slowly open out. He said, “Look, no more spring in it.” I asked, “What does that mean?” He answered, “I’ve gotten old.”
Happy birthday to you, Mr. Hecaitou!
Today is my 41st birthday.

Does this make me officially a middle-aged uncle? I don’t know. All I know is that I’ve finally reached the far side of forty, a distance I couldn’t imagine as a kid, deep inside the adult world. It’s nothing like I pictured. I can’t do everything, and I can’t do as I please. “Maturity” doesn’t buy you a settled life. It only throws light a little farther out, enough to show you how astonishingly ignorant you are. Every year now I get more done than the year before, and that pace will never catch the problems piling up. I’ve grown stronger, and the world has grown more complicated. Life is an exam you never finish, and it doesn’t get harder in a straight line.

After forty, life finally starts to look like a real film. What’s a real film? One where what the hero gains stays gained and what he loses stays lost. In your teens and twenties, life is more like a video game. Mess around as stupidly as you like, hit “restart” and everything’s back to normal. You can start over, because you never really got anything, so you can’t really lose anything, and it hardly matters how many times you fall. In your thirties, life starts to look like a stage play. Botch your performance and it’s no longer just your problem: everyone’s work that night is wasted. And once that night is over, it’s over for good. It won’t come again and it can’t be patched. But you can still fight to get the second night right, then the third, the fourth... People will forget the first night’s accident and take it for the rehearsal greatness requires.

A film can’t be reshot. Once it’s on the big screen it is what it is, and nobody can change it. After forty, they put the button in your hand, or you grab one and hug it to your chest. Press it and something real happens in the real world. Only now is a decision a real choice and responsibility a real weight. This time there’s no undo, no cancel, no rolling back to the last version. The world sits down across from you, takes five bullets out of a revolver, spins the cylinder hard, slaps the gun on the table and says: “This time, we do it for real!”

This is also why old men are so tiresome. Some of them always act as if they alone in all the world are facing that revolver. Everyone knows better, and some people are staring at a diesel chainsaw in the world’s hands. Others try to slip in a water pistol and put on a show of bravery, thinking nobody can tell, but everyone can see the water on their heads, and the water in them. Old men all share one worry nobody says out loud: you’ve spent your life on stage performing away to yourself, sure you’re the only lead. Then the shot rings out and you look down. No lead’s halo on you, there never was. Only shaft after shaft of light, coming through you from behind.

I can’t play the lead. I’m better as a supporting actor. The world is the lead, the internet the supporting actor; the internet is the lead, internet writing the supporting actor; internet writing is the lead, essayists and columnists the supporting actors. So I’m the supporting actor of the supporting actor of the supporting actor, on the frontier of the frontier of the frontier of the world. After all these years and all these words, I’ve learned one very simple thing: everything written to show off the self turns to ash, and everything written for other people stays in circulation. “Stranger, I Wait for You in Spring” and “The Promise: For a Reader” are still being read today, and people still come by to comment. All those pieces where I showed the crowd how to kill an opponent with one stroke went dead silent once the first excitement passed, and were forgotten without the least effort. Be the supporting actor in your own writing, write for a lead you’ve never met: that’s the only way to keep words alive. This world has far too many selves, and what’s precious is any self willing to give up its seat.

Every November 5 since 2003 I’ve written a piece wishing myself a happy birthday, and they’re probably the most self-regarding things I’ve ever written. When I went looking for them today, half had already dissolved into the internet. You see: the self keeps falling apart like this, and the only constant is change. Here are the seven I can still find, all together, as a gift for you: to thank you for your patience, and to mark all the years I’ve kept you company.
Thank you for reading “Monologue of a Supporting Actor.” Happy birthday to me!

Lately, every morning at dawn, an angel in robes whiter than snow stands at the head of my bed, pounds a gong, then bends down and bellows in my ear: “Get up! You’re nearly forty, aren’t you ashamed?” I know what he means. I should live more respectably. Be steady in speech and manner. Sip, don’t guzzle. Get up early, don’t linger in bed. Stop going to the sporting goods superstore once a year to bring home twelve identical XXXXL black T-shirts. My hair’s nearly gone, so at least pull in the gut and give the young some hope, so they don’t decide life after middle age is all disgrace, and every birthday from here on just another honorary award for living a long time.
Every birthday is a fresh bout of panic.

On October 15, something came over me and I wrote this: What’s it like to hit forty? It’s like sitting in a room with all four walls falling in on you. In your twenties and thirties you could still find a friend, have a drink and unload. At forty you look around, and all your friends are clawing their way out of the rubble. Bei Dao put it perfectly: now we drink deep into the night, and when our glasses touch, it’s the sound of dreams breaking.

I’ve finally become Uncle Caitou, a middle-aged man in a sorry state in a shattered life. It doesn’t sound nice, but it’s honest. I don’t believe in music, agarwood, yoga, Chinese medicine, red wine, bead bracelets, coffee, rinpoches, brush calligraphy, positive energy, frog-buttoned jackets or organic food, just as I refuse to read newspapers and magazines, watch TV, or open a Taobao shop. None of it will ever package me into an interesting middle-aged man at the dinner table. I used to dread running out of things to talk about, I lived in fear of killing the mood. Now I think just sitting here in silence is pretty good. Why, on a clear summer afternoon, with a good bottle of ice-cold beer, should you keep your mouth shut? There’s good reason for it. Enjoyment means avoiding every unnecessary drain. Such as understanding others, or being understood.

At forty you finally get a few of the perks of age. Overnight I cracked the mystery of red-braised beef, and the before and after were worlds apart. From one friend’s home to the next, from one round of admiration to the next, I do it fast and easy. The kitchen is my warded ground: no thinking, no hesitating, almost no control, and I’m always unhurried, with room to spare. It’s as if every plate of braised beef I’ve eaten in forty years has given up its secrets, as if time has bored clean through every cookbook and left only doing as I please. I don’t care whether the stove and pots are up to it or the seasonings all there, or where I’m starting from. I’m sure I’ll get where I meant to go.

Then it dawned on me that I’d already glazed everything in caramel, braised everything over a low flame, reduced everything over a high one. So I turned to clear stew. I tried for richer flavors with fewer seasonings: the corn in a pork rib soup, a clean sweetness sugar can’t give you, the high notes of a chord, the base notes of a perfume. The other side of mastery is taking things apart, and the perks of age mean you no longer get punished for it. It’s a rare privilege. Take off the roof, the windshield, the leather seat covers, the doors, the floor rubber, and see how far a car will still run. Most cars keep running, as it turns out, and a good deal faster. Something you could call “the origin of the world” is slowly showing itself, and you can see it without stooping so low as to bring the soul into it.

So the things I could say or not say, I no longer say. The words I could write or not write, I no longer write. The people I could see or not see, I no longer see. All that talk of subtraction in life is sheer madness. The river reaches the sea in the end, that’s all, so there’s no point laboring to add tributaries. When it comes down to it, I’m afraid of the bother.

I’ve heard you get two chances to turn your life around. One comes in middle age, when under crushing pressure you shake off the gloom and burst into flowers a hundred times more brilliant than youth. The other comes in old age, when you blaze up once more, bright enough to drive off the cold of death, like Matisse’s last building. At forty, I pray for one of them. After all, I took the road less traveled, and I don’t intend to put on a bow tie again, or to seek absolution anymore.
Ten companies texted me: Mr. He, we wish you a happy birthday. Download our app and get a birthday gift.
Hecaitou 2015.11.05

This past year was rough: one violent upheaval after another, several alarms in a single night. So every time I see those comments nitpicking my articles, I feel great admiration for myself. Whatever life throws at me, the articles stay smooth and graceful, no ups and downs on account of how I feel or what I’m going through. Even at my unhappiest, I can still write something that makes people howl with laughter.

Nobody notices. I write a lot and I write fast, so they take it for granted. Every evening at six, the article lands right on time. Who gives a thought to the morning milk and the evening paper in their housing complex? Who cares whether the milkman or the paperboy is fed and warm, or what mood he’s in? If it’s ever late, there’ll be complaints.

I don’t let any bad mood show, and I don’t have a Hecaitou of my own whose WeChat account I can go cry in. I write cheerfully, always, and when there’s honestly nothing worth writing about today, I pick a piece I like from my old blog and post that. From November 5 last year to today, I’ve written 354 articles. This is what they mean by doing a simple thing over and over. And how many people can do it?

The strangest stranger is often the one you see every day. I’m in touch with hundreds of thousands of people here through WeChat every day, more than ten million visits in all, and we’re still strangers. You’ve read so much, and you don’t know me at all.

I long ago stopped writing to be understood or to get recognition. I write because it’s my nature, the way it’s a horse’s nature to run. Give it a stretch of pasture and it’ll run, other horses or no other horses. I write because it makes me happy. When a piece is done, my mind runs clear and I’m quietly delighted. And since I broke away from circles large and small, I write with no scruples at all. No favors, no grudges, no cause and effect to get tangled in, so of course it flows.

When I started blogging I had just 400 readers. I called them the Four Hundred Blows, meaning four hundred hits a day. Time flew, and of those 400, probably not one in ten has stayed with me to this day. We drifted apart along the road; they couldn’t keep up. When I run into an old acquaintance now and then, most look haggard, worn out in body and mind, their old style gone. Only then do I realize I’m not the same as other people after all. I’m still here, but they’re all gone.

Other people have been living for decades, and I haven’t started. The kind of life they define, I haven’t so much as wet my toes in. As for intelligence, I don’t count as clever. My memory’s bad and I’m weak at math. From elementary school on, I was surrounded by big kids older, stronger and smarter than me. I had to work very hard and put in extra time just to draw even, or get half a body length ahead.

Someone asks: where’s your review plan? I can only stare, tongue-tied, no idea what they’re talking about. What’s review? What’s a plan? Neither existed in my world. You studied to beat this chapter so you could play the next one, so why review, why plan? Then I grew up and there were these things called career plans and life plans. I stared, tongue-tied, all over again. I’d muddled my way from a cubicle to a private office, so how would I know how to plan any of it? A home in the city, a living room in the home, a sofa in the living room, a TV across from the sofa: that’s about all most people’s life plans come to. With a TV you can go buy the things on the TV, and with a sofa you can lie there dreaming of one spur-of-the-moment trip after another, one spur-of-the-moment romance after another.
The dividing line is right here: do you reach out and take from a world of existing stock, or go explore a new one? It splits people cleanly into two groups, two worldviews.

In August I went to Europe with two friends for 21 days. We met at the airport, took one look at each other and roared with laughter: each of us had only a backpack and a small roller case, all carry-on, nothing to check. And we all had the same idea: if you’re missing something, buy it when you get there. Looking back, if the three of us hadn’t been like this, that trip to Europe would probably never have happened in our lifetimes.

The world is made of Lego bricks. Some people spend ten years going around a small circle, then pick up the bricks in that circle and start building their lives. Some spend decades roaming, in no hurry to build, wanting to find out how many kinds of brick there are in this world and all the ways they combine. So they can make castles and flying dragons, and create a new world on top of this Lego one. Walk into the land where no one has been, and you can create.

Pure innocence, pure madness and pure persistence can ignore the births and deaths of small-scale spaces and touch the truest rules of the world. The deepest mysteries live in the most common sayings. Ask me what I’ve learned from thirty-nine years of life, and it comes down to one word:
Banana!
