Today’s my birthday. In the small hours Chen Kun posted my new cartoon avatar on Weibo, and the congratulations came down in an avalanche. I posted on WeChat Moments and a lot of lurkers suddenly floated to the surface, quite a spectacular sight. I nearly decided to have a birthday once a week.

Suddenly I’m thirty-eight, with forty in sight, and it makes me anxious. It’s been five years since I left a state company at thirty-three and went drifting around on my own. I stepped off life’s main road with a pack on my back and a stick in my fist, and I’ve wandered the wilderness for five whole years. They’ve been longer than a lifetime.

This year, August 14 was the Qixi Festival. In the small hours I confirmed a few things, and everything hit me at once. I went downstairs for noodles, came back, and posted a long piece on WeChat Moments. It’s a true picture of my past year, so for my birthday I’m publishing it as a keepsake:
“I’m Eating Cart Noodles in the Rain”

Cart noodles from 7-Eleven, with chili sauce and a few fish balls rolling around. In the dark I can’t see the gold of the noodles, only the rain coming down and down. Falling on the thick leaves, falling on the black road, falling on the rooftops near and far, falling in the bowl too. The whole world is raining, and all the raindrops in the world are falling into my bowl.

I don’t mind at all, because I’m happy. A few hours ago I was miserable. Now I’m happy. Maybe I’ll wake up tomorrow and something new will knock me back into the abyss. Impermanence is that fast, that merciless. None of that matters now. This moment is enough. This bowl of noodles is plenty.

In these five years, the last time I was this happy was at Tencent, when project B4 got approved. I came downstairs as if in a dream, giddy all the way up, my bones half a pound lighter. That day I drank a few bottles of old Kingway, ice-cold, and floated through it. That night, I didn’t tell a single joke.

Then came the long five years, five times harder than I’d expected. I thought it would only be hard. I had no idea that above hard there were five more levels: arduous, painful, doubtful, despairing, and begging to die and not getting it. There may be more, but I haven’t met them yet, and I don’t know if I can keep taking it.

Fighting day and night, and above the battles, campaigns. Each new attempt brought a new failure, each new failure a new attempt. In that endless-looking loop, I joked that I was “fighting and failing and failing and fighting, one scheme falls through so I hatch another, it falls through and I hatch another.” I’m not afraid of failure, but there’s been so much of it that I’m afraid I’m about to be afraid.

So I’m this happy now not because I think I’m about to win, but because, in what looks like an endless struggle, I’ve moved a little farther from fear. Not by much. Just a little. From the outside you’d probably see nothing different. Only a patient gardener can sense a seed breaking its shell under the soil.

So there’s no one to share this moment with. What would I say? What could I say? And on a Qixi like this, on a rainy night like this. All I can do is be quietly happy by myself. I don’t have much money left, just enough to buy myself a bowl of cart noodles.

Right now, how many rooms in the world still have their lights on, and how many kinds of feeling are flooding the night? How many desires, large and small, are flaring up and dying, and how many people are awake listening to the rain, unable to sleep? Who’s talking, and who’s listening?
I’m eating cart noodles in the rain.

In the small hours of my thirty-eighth birthday, I thought of an afternoon twenty years ago, catching crayfish on the Pukou campus of Nanjing University. The silt came up to my thighs and the water was under ten degrees, but my burning hormones were a suit of armor, so I could reach bare-handed into a flooded hole up to the shoulder and pull out an angry crayfish. The sun was warm, the wind light, and at the edge of the field a bunch of friends stood waiting with plastic buckets, talking and laughing. When I turned sideways and stretched my arm down as far as it would go, my earlobe almost touching the water, their laughter sounded remote and unreal. Then my fingertips would feel a small stir in the water, and I could begin to wait, terrified. Within two seconds, a huge claw, red to almost black, would strike and clamp onto my palm and not let go. I’d grip both claws, drag it out and fling it into the bucket. A cheer would go up from the bank, and everyone would crowd around marveling at its size, its strength. I stood barefoot in the mud and turned my palm over, watching the dark red blood push through the yellow-brown silt bit by bit and run slowly down with the muddy water. Only then did my frozen, numb hand begin to feel the first trace of pain.
About half a year later, that summer, I found out you catch crayfish with a line. Nobody uses their hands.

The crisscrossing wounds on my palm all healed without a mark. Even with skin that scars badly, after all these years those scars have quietly gone. Compared with the other stupid things boys do, catching crayfish was one of the better ones. The round scars you burn with a match to show courage last a lifetime, and tattoos pricked with a needle dipped in blue-black ink only get uglier with the years. I never tried any of that, because I’m afraid of pain. But I wasn’t afraid of crayfish, probably because the first kind of pain can be foreseen, while the second, unforeseeable, hides a huge excitement: those flooded holes might also hold soft-shelled turtles and water snakes. And because the instant you grip those claws is like making a covenant with the underwater world. I’m a visitor to the unknown, and the handshake is how we talk. Burns and tattoos are a sacrifice, homage to the distant adult world, a declaration that you have the nerve to enter. What I am and what I have has never interested me much.

I’m thirty-eight today, many years into the adult world. An all-powerful adult world doesn’t exist. Neither does a frame of mind that handles life with room to spare. Many questions you couldn’t answer as a child still have no answers. People just stop asking. As a child you thought growing up would solve your troubles, that money, strength and a grown-up’s looks would solve them. Most of them did get solved, but the price turns out to be more trouble still. Because you’re no longer the one catching crayfish. You yourself are the crayfish.

You need to dig a hole fast and hide in it. You have to make the burrow long and deep so you won’t be easily caught. Then it’s not enough, and you want more exits: one near the water, one near the field, one with a view. You dig so hard that sometimes you break through the ridge of the field and let all the water out, and then you’re terribly punished. The other crayfish look on coldly and shrug: bad luck. The burrows get dug and collapse, collapse and get dug again. At last you have an underwater palace with passages in every direction, only to find that the best time of your life was strolling underwater with another crayfish, claws lightly linked, when the two of you didn’t even have one burrow.

In twenty years I’ve abandoned several holes halfway, because halfway through I can’t stop asking: what am I doing? Is this what I want? The answer has always been no. So I ask again: what makes a crayfish dig mud year after year? The answer is expectation. Expecting more food, bigger water, prettier views. Expectation’s other name is fear: fear of famine, fear of confinement, fear that none of what you expect will happen. So you keep digging. I find that explanation more convincing. Fear keeps people on the track they’re already on, inside the rules, as if things have been this way since the world began. There are other ways out, other choices. But what those choices might cost is enough to frighten people out of their reason.
Crustaceans can fly too. At least that’s what they say in “StarCraft.”

The people around me are going quiet as they near forty. Whatever they once expected, at this age they find they’re losing more, and faster. Everything they could rely on works less well now, to varying degrees. Ideals have become a stimulant you hand other people. Passion still gives you a moment’s excitement, but seems to end in ash all the same. Eternal greed is a little better, but it’s also the easiest to get sick of. Even desire, when it can’t get you moving anymore, or moving achieves very little, becomes a source of depression. Odd how things turn out. Your “three views” (of life, of values, of the world), which you sneered at in your teens, have become something hard and real. Your three views, how you see yourself, society and the world, decide how long your drive can burn and how far it can carry you. Ideals, passion, desire, luck and the cleverness you think you have all run out at this stage, and you’re left floating in a vast blank silence. “Hi, what’s new with you today?”

Before thirty-five, you always feel there’s still time, plenty of chances, plenty of years. After thirty-five, the drumbeat of fate gets faster and the hourglass pours down like a waterfall. There isn’t enough time. What should you do? The time for looking for answers is long past. Now it’s time to answer. Life’s endless questions come surging in, you can’t even look up, you just write as hard as you can to fill the exam paper. Everything you thought you’d figured out, all those conclusions in your hands, now gets tested, and most of it will be smashed to pieces. They’re all things you borrowed from other people over your first thirty years, and few of them were ever yours. The day of repayment has come. What will you stand on to reach the next thirty years?
Borges said: The god of fate has no pity, and God’s long night has no end. Your flesh is only time, time ceaselessly passing, and you are nothing but each solitary instant.
Happy birthday! Mr. Hecaitou!

Today I turn thirty-seven. I’d meant to say, “Don’t be afraid of your thirties, because very soon you’ll start worrying about forty creeping up.” That pretty quip suits Weibo, but it doesn’t belong here. It doesn’t go like this: you’ve gained experience, picked up titles, even a touch of wisdom, so you can live a little easier, move through society with room to spare, and start enjoying the perks of maturity. It doesn’t go like that at all. After thirty-five it feels more as if you’ve finished basic training and life is about to give you the real thing. The weight somersaults upward within a few short years, and the world hasn’t settled down either: it spins more madly by the day. You don’t seem to have any choice but to hold on. But under that load you can’t help a faint worry that at some moment you’ll go down, just like that, all at once.

In my twenties it felt as if I was opening my arms and going out to meet the world. In my thirties, the whole world tips over onto you. You can hear your joints crackle, and you hold your breath, not daring to let up for a second. The pressure comes from every direction, but it no longer costs you physical strength, or even calls on your intelligence. It just wears you down, so the white hair can grow wild at your temples. I think this stage of life calls for honesty, the kind it takes to accept the weights life’s changes bring. If life’s hammer has beaten you again and again into a piece of glowing red copper, then look like a piece of copper. Don’t explain it as a fire inside you, and don’t promise you’ll stay hard. Hardness and sharpness can get you as far as today, but I suspect what comes next will require only toughness.

How to make sense of this change? When you’re young and green, the world is made of doors. Push them open slowly or kick them in with a flying foot: those are the years of brute force. There are infinite doors and infinite possibilities behind them. But after enough exploring you finally understand: you can’t spend a whole life opening doors. There must be one door, or a few, that lead into a deeper, farther world. Whether you entrust yourself to wisdom or to pure desire, you’ll follow it all the way, and it’s part of you. You can work at it and reach the place you’ve settled on before your hourglass empties. And because of that, you stop envying the doors other people chose and the roads they walked. Knowing the limit of what you can do is where the frantic mind begins to rest, but it doesn’t make you very happy.

Because a lot of things break down. Some things you took to be solid, even beautiful, soon shatter. Once you really grasp that everyone’s time is limited, you quickly see what everyone on stage is in such a hurry for. Plenty of pretty big words can’t hold up anymore, and plenty of pretty people show what they really are. You see that only the laws of survival are at work. Some of what they drive is just more deceptive, and some is quicker to show the dagger. Of everything, ask: what does he, or it, live off? “What do you live off?” is a sharp knife, perfect for cutting appearance from substance. With the pieces all over the ground, you find that few things deserve to be called real problems, or pure ideas. The excitement you once chased was a kaleidoscope: under the dazzle there are only three mirrors and some scraps of paper, powerless against reality.
And what’s my own reality?

I have a study now, with three pots of green plants on the bookshelf. Because of the smoke they’re all feeble, and their leaves never manage to hang down over the top shelf as planned. On the desk is a laptop with a few books always stacked beside it. I finish one and take it away. New ones arrive and go on the pile. Between the books and the computer lie countless adapters, cables, chargers and small gadgets. In the middle a blue plastic box stands out, holding a translucent rubber mouth guard called an “anti-snoring device,” said to prevent apnea. Nobody in their twenties worries about apnea, but at my age I have to start biting down on a mouth guard like a boxer, and even my sleep has become a deadly ring. I always hoped to go through life “armed to the teeth.” I didn’t know it would be this kind of armament.

The desk displays what I already have, in the glow of greed. The anti-snoring device is the fear of death, and that shadow is closing in. Thirty-five may be the average human lifespan across history, and over millions of years the number may be smaller still. So even if people today can live to seventy or eighty, some fears are already written into our DNA. Smallpox and tuberculosis are far behind us, but reach that average age and you still panic for no reason. Add the so-called zodiac year. If you also happen to have picked a harder road in your career, you always feel weighed down, and you don’t know why. Meanwhile your friends and acquaintances are having babies, your parents are getting old, and the tides of life bring an autumn bleakness. When people have children at this point, it’s less that they’re giving a child life than that the newborn lights up their own and drives off the shadow of death. I watch my friends, full of feeling, write words deep and shallow for their children. It’s all for themselves, really. It revalues their middle-aged lives. It seems to tie them to a more distant future and give them some worth through responsibility. Living for other people may be a nuisance, but if you don’t have to, you need a greater weight to keep your soul from flying off on the wind. So the young man who ran so far starts slowly back along the same road. Some people say: I was surprised to find I’d become the kind of person I despised when I was young. Maybe so. It’s just that back then life didn’t weigh very much yet.

I’ve noticed plenty of changes, including one extra trip to the toilet at night and the stomach medicine kept on my desk. I used to believe all discomfort was temporary, that a good night’s sleep might fix it. Even if it didn’t, I was sure the day would come. I don’t think so now. I’ve begun to believe I may have to carry these aches with me from here on. That’s no fun, of course, but it has to be accepted as part of life, the way a tree goes on growing with its knots. It keeps growing, with all its uncomfortable people and things. The tree just stands there, and there doesn’t seem to be any other choice. After chasing a beautiful world for so long, I’m trying to live alongside one that’s less than perfect. When I see the world’s dark wounds again, I think more about the matching scars on me, about how we mirror each other, about how I can’t possibly ascend into pure light.

A zodiac year brings many choices, yet the almanac says nothing is advisable. With all this pressure, fatigue, pain and fear, why keep walking, and walk where? A few days ago I was drinking with old friends, and one of them, older than me, talked about his business. After enormous hardship he’d finally won a bid and signed the contract. But as soon as he got to the site, a young woman from the client’s side, more than twenty years his junior, cursed him out and humiliated him. He admitted that in that instant he badly wanted to work out how much money he’d made over the years and, if it had reached the floor he’d set himself, quit at once and do nothing anymore. And in that same flash he was shocked by the thought: “How did I become this kind of person?” My old friend broke down on the spot, his face wet with tears of shame. Worse than pressure is betraying yourself. And the hard part is that at this age, even if you do it, nobody can blame you. They may even praise you for being practical, for knowing when to advance and when to withdraw.

I’d rather go on living a little emptily, unable to see what things will be like in ten years. Keeping alive the possibility that everything could be gone overnight lets you walk a little faster, a little farther. Like my old friend and the others: face your desires honestly, defend your taste firmly, then be hard on your own cowardice. You chose this door yourself, so you have to walk it to the end. We’re so imperfect, and yet so tough. There’s a time for weakness, a time for frailty, but the flower still has to open.

I turned thirty-five today. Five years ago I was thinking: how can I possibly be thirty? Now I’ve pretty much adapted to my thirties and shamelessly taken up the role of “Uncle He.” With it came the usual heap of thirty-something ailments: gout that flared up this year and put me in a wheelchair for four days, and a lower back and neck that hurt now and then. I used to be limber enough to stand with straight legs and press two neat palm prints on the floor. Not anymore. I don’t know if my joints have stiffened or my belly has grown. Either way, I’ve bought a lot of slip-ons with no laces.

As you can tell from that first paragraph, at thirty-five you give off a slack, lazy air. This age is a fat, clingy cat. Yet life keeps changing fast, especially for someone like me. No year of my life has had this much happen in it: first I was too busy to find time for my Blog, then too busy to be in the mood. Reach your mid-thirties, hair falling out, belly pushing forward, face starting to sag, and people take you for an expert. They rush to give you a title, then haul you onto all kinds of stages to get some use out of you. Life settles down too. People bring you bits of work or ask you for a favor, and you stop asking yourself “how am I going to survive?”

I asked that question for a long time after I came to Beijing. Very young, I picked up the idea that everyone in this country had to have a work unit to live a stable, healthy life. Only people who’d done something bad, or the poor wretches in capitalist countries, had no unit to look after them and had to keep looking for jobs and changing jobs. Two years ago I had a unit. A unit is an imperial pardon, a get-out-of-execution card: it guarantees you a life and seals you off from the storm outside, from not knowing if you’ll last till evening. When I chose to walk out into the rain, fear closed over me and I felt I’d lost my protection. I’m ashamed to admit that at first I often missed being sheltered. Two years after my release into the wild, after more than 700 days and nights of rewilding, I still don’t know what tomorrow will bring and I still can’t answer that question. I’ve never had a schedule or a career plan. But for some reason I’ve been spared the fear of losing a unit. I wouldn’t say I’ve fallen in love with the storm, or with not knowing if I’ll last till evening, but I’ve gotten used to it. Picture a carnivore on the grassland, lying on a rock with its eyes half closed in the wind and sun, lazily licking its fur. You can’t say it loves or doesn’t love what’s in front of it. For it, there’s nothing but that rock, and then, licking fur.

Society took me in. I won’t call it generous and merciful, or next I’d have to spout all that gratitude crap with the snot and tears running together, but it did give me a chance. That matters more than anything; without it you have no choice of road. Imagine it otherwise: you dare step out of your warm, comfortable house, so a thunderbolt has to strike you on the spot, make a cautionary example of you and burn you down to a line of gray letters: See that? You still dare, you little shit? A society like that really would make people despair. My own experience gave me a different kind of confidence: work honestly, work seriously, and you might get a chance. In other words, you can issue yourself a job and provide your own living without ending up pale with hunger and in rags, leaving the onlookers terrified of the road you took. It’s a pretty good life. I often sing the pop hit “The Love Trade” at the top of my voice, alone at home. My point is that you can still sing “The Love Trade” in a world of nothing but work-unit people, just not with my earth-shaking, surging heroism.

I also ran some experiments on myself. In my first eleven years of work I saw plenty of scheming, cunning and trickery, all passed off as management with Chinese characteristics. The only question was whether you had one powerful daddy or a whole bunch of them. A leader’s authority was built from pressure, handouts, divide-and-rule, punishment and sowing discord. The led were ignorant, weak sheep who needed a strong hand and military-style management to squeeze the most out of them. On my team, everyone could speak, and anyone could ask: why are we doing this? From the day I arrived to the day I left, that did no harm to my authority. At least I believe my team laughed more than any other and had a good time. It didn’t seem to hurt total output either. The key was that they enjoyed the work and felt it meant something. In fact, they did even better when I wasn’t there. So much so that I often joked: please keep this a secret, or the company will decide it shouldn’t be paying me.

Working with a post-80s team, even a post-85 team, is a pleasure, and so is working for my post-80s boss. Before this I worked with people born in the fifties and sixties, and the happiest day of that can’t touch the worst day of these two years. If I’d never left my little old world, I’d probably never have known that human relations can be that simple and management that painless, or believed that Chinese people could manage themselves and actually get something done together with no infighting. Don’t treat your subordinates as idiots, always tell them the truth, let them get on with the work they like: I don’t get why management studies needs so many books. From blue-green algae to humans, living things come with no instruction manual. This convinces me the future will be different, because the people building this society have changed, and so has the way they organize. New generations will keep growing up who don’t read Zeng Guofan management books, who don’t study going to work as the art of war. So why shouldn’t I hope to live a slightly more normal social life in my old age? When growing up replaces taming, people become people, and the world gets much softer and much better for it. We’ll no longer be comrade wolves to one another.

The price, of course, is less time for my Blog. First there was no time, then no mood. Ten years ago and earlier, I had an internet ideal. I still have it, but it’s changed a lot. I used to think the online world was an ideal republic, a utopia, and naively thought people online all had the same temperament. Now I understand I thought so because I wanted to escape. With over three hundred million people online, it’s the crowd you can’t avoid, the life with nowhere to hide. You used to be able to flee the crowd by going online. Now everyone’s met again on the internet, and you have to try to understand what they’re thinking and doing. Especially when you build internet products, where everything contradicts what you took for “common sense.” Hardly anyone’s online range goes past 10 websites, which means a few thousand people a day. A network of 50,000 people and a network of 50 million are two different worlds. The experience and theorems of a small world are useless in front of the great mass of people. Likewise, the minority who go online and the great mass who never do are miles apart in how they behave and what they think.

For the people who faithfully read my Blog, I’ve pretty much said what I had to say. To keep going I might have to switch vehicles: a novel, say, or a script. As for the vast general public, I still haven’t found the language that reaches them. I’ve tried a few things, and they didn’t go well. The ones that did work only made me sadder; there was no point in doing it that way. So I’d rather put more effort into the “Tree Hollow” project. Everyone’s life story is a book. Let people tell their own, and I can sit quietly in the audience. In my internet ideal, getting everyone to dare to speak matters far more than how brilliantly I speak.

What I thought about most this past year was this: how to give all those timid, bashful ordinary people, who curl up at the slightest touch, the courage to say something. How to create a place where they can say it and feel at ease. How to keep up an atmosphere where they can make something of their own, spark off each other, share it, and feel that this small thing made someone happy for a day and stayed on someone’s mind for a night. How to get them to admit, bravely, that their own lives and their own words have value, that there’s nothing to be ashamed of, that it’s worth writing down, so that in the long stream of time they can answer to themselves. I don’t know how yet. But for me, this is my internet ideal.
Thirty-five now. In the year ahead I hope to finish a new book, write a script, and do one thing I’ve never done before.
Midnight passed and I turned thirty-three. I opened my Blog and dug up every birthday post I’ve written since I started:

2003, age 28: “November 5”; 2004, age 29: “High-Speed Orbit Change: Written at the Edge of Twenty-Nine”; 2005, age 30: “Year One of Quitting Smoking, September 10, Thoughts at Thirty”; 2006, age 31: “Bit Sea Log, August 9, Happy Birthday to Me”; 2007, age 32: “Bit Sea Log, Month 20 Day 3, 32 Today.”

As the list shows, since my first Blog post, “D-day,” on September 15, 2003, I’ve been at this more than five years and spent 5 birthdays in the Blog. Not counting what I wrote on Paowang and Niubo, that’s 3,944 posts. Writing and writing, I’ve reached thirty-three, the same age the captain in “La Grande Vadrouille” gives when the nun asks him in the convent.

Add up the time and energy these posts took and it’s no small number. Of course you’ll ask: was it worth it? I don’t want to answer that. Just look at the posts listed above, click through and read the Chinese in them. You’ll find a guy called Hecaitou, five years of his life, how he lived them, where he went, who he met, what happened. That’s the power of a Blog. A post or two, a month or two, may not show much. But choose to keep a record, keep it up year after year, and what comes out is a personal chronicle. It isn’t a history textbook or a media record. It tells an ordinary person’s story: his joys, angers and sorrows, what life dealt him, what he came to understand, the traces he left passing through this world, and how he slowly changed, bit by bit, into what he is today.
Now and then I leaf through my old posts, afraid that somewhere along the way I’ve lost myself.

A lot changed between thirty-two and thirty-three. I got sick, finished my work in Lijiang, and finally made it back to Kunming. I quit the company I’d served for eleven years and came to Beijing empty-handed to become a Beijing drifter. My nearsightedness went up to 650 degrees, and my weight bounced between 92 and 105 kilograms. This past year I saw the snow disaster, the earthquake, the Olympic uproar and the global economic crisis now under way. My family also welcomed two newborns and held a wedding. Because of work, I missed them all.

I left a safe state company and the protection of the system at a time like this, walked out the door with a backpack and ran straight into an economic crisis. You ask how I feel now? I have exited the capsule and I feel fine. The biggest crisis isn’t the economic one. It’s the one deep inside me. It started brewing eleven years ago and broke out this May, and by the time the subprime crisis began this July, my personal crisis was already over. Once you know how you want to live your life and where you fit in the world, what’s left is calm. The whole world could crumble to mud in the next second and it wouldn’t matter. Whether I should have quit and how I’ll survive out here aren’t questions anymore, and not worth my time. Had I not chosen and acted, I might be patting my chest now, crying out how lucky I was. But right after that I’d be fretting that the old company had lost a massive 2.5 billion yuan with a debt ratio over 98%, then fuming over the pay cut, and finally thinking, “If I went out there, then...”

A donkey can’t stand between two piles of hay forever, not knowing which way to go. It has to pick one, walk over and eat. And eat as if it’s the only pile of hay in the world. Whether there’s enough and how long it lasts don’t matter. What matters is not eating the wrong one, and then being wrong for many years.

Compared with Kunming, by any measure of comfort or luxury, my life in Beijing looks as if the economic crisis really had hit me. Outside of college, I’ve never used a toilet or lived in a room that small, never ridden public transit this often, and my bookshelf holds fewer than 30 books. But my state of mind? No stretch of the past eleven years has had me this excited and fired up. I skip up the stairs humming a little tune. The wealth and languor of the past put me through torment; the lack and strain of now have made me calm, and full of life.

It’s a bit like elementary school, when I couldn’t wait to get there each morning for the new things to learn and new toys to play with. In a place like Beijing, as long as you don’t keep your eyes fixed on other people’s houses, cars and women, and don’t sit there straining to be this or that, there’s plenty worth learning and living through, and plenty of joy in it. All through the 90s, people wanted “to be a genius.” In the first decade of the 21st century, the goal was “to be Newbe” (my spelling of niubi, Chinese for badass). But I’ve looked into it: Newbe exists only in the comparative. There is no Newbest (a very good domain name, too bad it’s already registered).

I once said you’re better off treating the internet as a long spiritual practice. Now, on my thirty-third birthday, I’d add: you might as well treat life as endless learning. So today I wish Hecaitou the student a happy birthday, and may he carry on with his practice and his learning.

A 10th birthday brings despair. School has no end in sight. You’re only halfway through elementary, with six years of middle and high school to come, then four of college, before you can leave for good and have nobody in charge of you. A small mind starts counting up 13 years and seems to be looking at the end of time. No 10-year-old can imagine what 13 years means. When everyone has gone, you wash your hands and feet, climb into bed, pull up the covers and lie in the dark, and all you can do is let out one small sigh.

A 20th birthday brings a thrill you can’t explain. The long, dark tunnel is nearly over. You can see daylight ahead, you can even smell the grass, and you can’t help leaping on the spot and snorting like a horse. You picture graduation day: the black gown, the cap and the books thrown higher than the sky. You want to run up somewhere high, somewhere you can see the whole city, and stand in the wind and shout: World, here I come! But on the actual day it rains, the class monitor is too late renting the gowns, and everyone ends up on the steel bleachers in loud T-shirts having their picture taken. It’s over before you’ve arranged your face, because other departments’ graduates are lined up waiting.

A 30th birthday brings sheer panic. You look away for a moment and suddenly you’re thirty. Few twenty-year-olds really believe this day will come. They’re still young, they have loads of time, they can wander around the world a while longer, just a while, and then they’ll pull themselves together and get ready to live seriously. But Thirty doesn’t wait for anyone. He rings the doorbell right on time, in a three-piece suit and gleaming shoes, stern and composed, and the first thing he says as he walks in is: So tell me, what have you done with all these years? A 30th birthday of gaping and stammering, of good wishes that make you squirm, of a wish made in a fluster. There’s no time, nothing’s ready, and in the scramble you’re suddenly thirty. One sentence goes round and round at the bottom of your mind, perfectly clear: I’m still a kid!

Not many people want a 40th birthday. Every birthday after forty reminds you that you’ve passed the summit and everything’s begun to decay, and only the view ahead keeps rising, step by step. And 40 isn’t a big enough number to be an honor, to stand for experience, wisdom, achievement and long life. So after forty, many people stop celebrating their own. They’d rather do it for their children, and let the candles on a child’s cake light up their own future. They’d rather do it for the old, with pink longevity peaches, always in even numbers, for the years they’ve kept each other company. At this age, every flutter means danger on all sides and every contentment is about to vanish, so you keep away from birthdays, away from ecstasy and excitement. Happiness is just this: no wind, no rain, no clear sky either. A mood neither high nor low, neither good nor bad, life’s pressure and drive just about in balance. You don’t expect the pressure to jump and you don’t dream of endless drive. You only hope this moment of peace will stay one more second, one more second, and that’ll be enough. You only hope the world and fate won’t turn their faces and notice you. Don’t make a sound, don’t notice me, let me get to old age in peace.

Every time a birthday comes around, people look back and dream of reversing time’s arrow and dodging the decay that’s coming. But all they can do is go through the good things in memory one more time and sigh at how the years slip by and don’t come back. What if time really could run backward?

On your 40th birthday, you’re getting ready to head for 30. You watch your parents grow younger and healthier, bit by bit, while your child gets smaller and smaller and finally disappears from your life. The skills, experience and money you built your family with drain away. You slowly forget how deftly you once handled work and life, you’re back to finding your way, and everything turns fresh and vivid again. So on someone’s 40th birthday, wish him another start on the road, another setting out for adventure, and that this time he catches the scenery he missed.

On your 30th birthday, you no longer have to be established by thirty, as Confucius demanded. The hair you lost grows back. The old lovers lost in the crowd come back around. All the resentment and disgust gradually fade, you’re burning with love again, and then it all runs backward, back to the very first glance. Marching toward 20, you’re let off an adult’s responsibilities bit by bit. You’re forgiven more, and you see more patience and hope in other people’s eyes. Life gets easier and lighter. Once more you want to love, to eat, to run. And once more your wallet’s empty. People at your birthday party raise their beers and loudly wish you many more years of being broke and happy.

On your 20th birthday, you’ve forgotten most of the world’s evil and complication. Your appetite’s back, and you think all day about your next meal. Your sex drive’s back, and you feel like a walking pile driver. You return to the familiar campus, the familiar people and things, and see them differently. In the one you took for a fool, this time you may spot astonishing potential. In the little circle you worked so hard to break into, you may see only shallowness and boredom. You open your textbooks and have to admit that after all these years, this is the first time you’ve understood them, what the authors were trying to tell you. It dawns on you. Inside you, the world slowly sheds its surface, and you see the vast pulse under the rock and the racing magma. At last you understand how it runs, and what sleight of hand it uses to hide the truth.

On your 10th birthday, you’re on your little bed, sitting alone in the dark. In a void no one else can see, you clearly see the dense lines of cause and effect, one end tied to the present, the other to the distant future. Deep in your mind, the seeds lie in neat rows, every one countable, and 10, 20, 30 years ago you saw them grown. The watercolor in your bedroom, the one you painted yourself, is the blue dragonfly you saw in the garden the day before yesterday. The song you liked best to sing at 40 has a stretch of melody your mother once sang softly in your ear through countless of your sleeps. Your home looks the way it does because you’ve built it countless times in blocks, and thinking how long it’ll be before you can make it real, you push them over in a temper, again and again...

Everyone lives in their own three lifetimes, going through past, present and future at once in every moment. Anything we do now, anything we say, any thought we have, comes from the distant past, from that distant me, and will reach into the distant future, to that me who hasn’t arrived. That’s what a birthday means. It isn’t a timestamp or an anniversary. It’s just a pause button: we fast-forward or play back, and set down the self of this moment between past and future.
Happy birthday to you today, and happy non-birthdays to you all the rest!
If I could cross the fog of time right now and stand in front of my 20-year-old self, what would I say to him?

It would be Nanjing, 1996, 22 Hankou Road, the classroom building at the end of the tree-lined avenue in North Garden. “Fluid Mechanics” is in session. Professor Jiang is at the blackboard on the conservation of vorticity, pointing at his chalk lines and asking the students to see how a vortex tube bends in space. White chalk dust crumbles down under his thick fingers. The main building has two kinds of chalk: a coarse, brittle one, which is white, and a fine, dense one, which is colored. All of it looks a little dull, because the sunlight comes into the room bent through the shade of the huge plane trees outside, along with the cicadas, and the air holds a green beyond counting.

I’m not listening. Nearly 12, and I’m hungry. Any hope of getting in line this week to play on the computer at the computer science guys’ rented room? Better not Saturday: that’s film appreciation, my favorite class, and we get “A River Runs Through It.” Of course, if I go to the rented room I’ll have to buy a salted duck. Just got paid for last month’s tutoring, plus my work-study money from the library, so that should cover it, with some jellied pork and a few bottles of Jinling dry beer on top. Can’t spend too much or there’s no cigarette money again this month, and Shancha are not fit for humans. Oh right, speaking class tomorrow night, I get to see GII again, and afterward we’ll probably get hauled off to a bar for whiskey and a disco to dance. Damn, I’ve finished the six library books, have to grab a few more on the way to the canteen. Don’t feel like going to class this afternoon...

I watch him wolf down a pound of rice and two pork chops, right down to the cabbage stalks and gravy underneath. I watch him use his work-study job to take six books out of the library every 2 days and read them all night by candle in the dorm, the flame scorching one big hole after another in his mosquito net. I watch him pack his schedule solid: odd jobs, travel, chess, music, movies, social practice programs, getaways for buddies who’ve been in fights... A mad spinning top that can’t stop for a moment. He opens his greedy eyes on every color the world has. He wants to put a hand on everything, go up and take a bite of everything. His interest in this world is like his permanently starving stomach: it’s never had enough.

He can’t see me. He’s too busy. Even standing right in front of him, with more or less his face, I wouldn’t get noticed. To him the world has too many wonders to stop for, and even so he’s often bored. How would he notice an ordinary middle-aged man, the kind of adult he hates most, with his self-satisfied fat and the odious smell of the grown-up world? He walks past me without a moment’s pause, still quick as the wind in his flip-flops. His big shorts flap, and the flip-flops smack against his soles, a crisp “slap, slap.”
I want to call out to him and tell him:

Go ask Jiang, from 206 in physics, to get a meal with you. You two will become good friends in your last year of college, and it’ll last a lifetime. What you don’t know yet is that he won’t have a 40th birthday. This is the longest stretch of time you’ll ever spend together. After this you’ll lose each other on the streets of Beijing again and again, and find each other again and again. And then, suddenly, there is no then.

Spend more time with your girlfriend. Your days have already started counting down and you have no idea. Right now her clinging annoys you, and you’d rather be playing computer games with the guys. You both think this will go on and on. It won’t. In a little over two years you’ll break up at the train station and never see each other again in this life. For many years after that, guilt will take human form and turn up in countless dreams, asking you over and over: Did you do your best? What did you ever change for her?

Watch out for those bastards in physics and computer science. A year from now they’ll take you over the wall at midnight into the physics building and get online on a thesis adviser’s computer. It’ll change your life for good: from then on, you’re tied to the internet. Over the years you’ll slowly turn into a strange half-human, half-network creature. By then you’ll be calling yourself “Hecaitou,” and thinking it’s just an ID, a code name. But it’ll slowly eat your personality and get you used to existing its way. You’ll search the net without a moment’s break and keep refreshing your phone. You’ll jump from link to link through endless information, make countless pieces of content for that world and get drunk on it, more than ten years of frenzy, with no sign yet of it going out.

Because of it you’ll be able to do what others can’t, and because of it you’ll lose the life others get to live. So be careful of that night. When they ask, please think one second longer. Even if it makes me vanish completely, you should stay one second longer. That’s a major fork in the road. If you don’t go that night, you’ll live a different life, a more human life. Not so much pain, and of course not so much ecstasy. You’ll need other people and be needed by them. Your life will be tangled up with other people’s through living, not through network cables and repeaters. You’ll be an ordinary fat guy, but you may be much happier than now, and feel more of what normal people feel.

You’re right about one thing: you won’t be just a spectator of this colorful world. You’ll get into it. Yes, just like your private fantasies back then, it happens. You’ll enter the worlds you now see in newspapers, on the radio and on TV, instead of gazing at them from far off and taking whatever they hand you. Until that day, everything you worry about now, this life you find pointless and flat, all has its purpose. Compared with twenty years later, this moment is plenty bright already. You just don’t have the means to consume most of it, which is why you so often feel low and powerless, and why the life in front of you seems boring.

Twenty years from now, you’ll understand that the real fun is in making these colors. The longing you held down in your early years will burst out of your hands once you’re able to make them. It takes much longer than admiring and taking in, and it’s much harder. It takes years of trying before you stumble on a tiny bit of progress, and you still don’t know if it’s in the right direction. Defeat, dejection, despair and self-doubt go with you the whole way, the normal state of that road. But it’s because of them that the final joy turns into ecstasy, and that in the ecstasy you at last feel a vast quiet. I have to admit, there’ll be a few moments like that, when you really do get some peace of mind and sleep deeply that night.

What I do want to remind you: along the way, hold on to yourself, and don’t lightly stray off your path. Whatever road you pick, the best choice is to walk it to the end. Don’t hesitate along the way, much less linger in hesitation, because that wastes too much of life. By the time you get back on the road, it may have cost you all of eleven years, and then there won’t be much time left to experience life. If a voice inside you calls, answer it. Don’t weigh gain and loss, success and failure, like a middle-aged man. Otherwise sooner or later you’ll find that every today you waste in indecision is eating up, a hundredfold, the human happiness you might have had. What you fear today about tomorrow mostly won’t happen once you act. But if you stand silent, then when tomorrow comes, the fear will show up as punishment and disaster, and that’s the most frightening thing of all. Because by then you’ll have nothing left to hold it off with: you’ve already wasted your yesterday.

But I won’t tell you any of this. Because even stumbling and staggering like that, you’ll still make it here to me. What you’re meant to lose, you’ll lose. What you’re meant to miss, you’ll miss. The traps you’re meant to fall into, you’ll fall into, and fall into again and again. And still you’ll come through, still you’ll reach me. Even if I could talk to you, change every parameter of fate, give you subtle hints or flat-out warnings, you wouldn’t save a moment. Because in the furnace of life, we’re copper. However we carry on, the hammering won’t be one second shorter. I can only look at you sadly, watch you walk through those regrets again, see them happen, and imagine that another road might have had other scenery. I look at you on the far side of the fog of time, and I want to say: though you’re so stupid it breaks my heart, I still love you.
Finally, the one thing I’m willing to tell you: whichever life you pick, you’ll still be a fat guy. Please don’t trouble yourself thinking about this one. Just accept it calmly.
